Comment: current building:
During speeches (especially when it’s someone who is not used to talking like a bar mitzvah), people are coming in and out of the room. Every time the door opens, the noise from the halls comes into the room. 

There is a simple and cheap way to reduce noise in the sanctuary that many shuls use. Put a sign on the outside of the sanctuary door that says something like “speech in progress, don’t enter”. It can be attached with Velcro or magnets or nail  and can easily be flipped to another side that says “enter quietly, services in progress”.
Comment: one improvement:
For me, more recognition and initiatives for those of us without kids. Also events for career connections and guidance. Its great that the shul is so focused on families, but the rest of us struggle to make friends and connections. 

For others - Cubbies are a simple way to make people happy and raise a few thousand dollars each year for the shul. The shul already has a coat closet in the front room that is barely used and would be perfect for this. Take down the closet doors and add wooden shelving and nametags. Make 2 sizes of cubbies (small = rectangle fits talis bag, large = square fits talis bag and diaper bag or folded up coats.) Rent them out for around $150-$400 per year. The regulars will absolutely love having an official space to keep their items, instead of having to lug them back and forth.
Comment: building fund:
Obviously the shul is ready to expand and this will cost a lot. However, the way the shul approached it seems unorganized and didn’t consider the financial situation of the community at large. Why is it that we haven’t seen one fundraising initiative outside of a large bill? 

There are many ways to fundraise and entice people to donate with events, dedications, and advertising. Asking for a SUGGESTED DONATION from members should be a last step after you already raised money, got people excited about the project, and know exactly how much you still need. People who can afford it will gladly pay extra to dedicate every door and bench. Those that are struggling won’t feel obligated to pay and will be more likely to donate if their situation improves. We may even donate our time or connections, if you don’t push us away. 

Donating to the shul is a choice that people make based on their financial capabilities. This is not a rich community. Many of the shul members can’t afford to own their own homes or struggle to pay a monthly mortgage. Even basic shul membership is a choice that is not easy to make. When we see a bill for the equivalent of 3 months rent on top of the membership we struggle to pay, it causes a lot of unnecessary anxiety, guilt and embarrassment. (Obviously we are obligated to pay this amount, but a unsettled bill still makes us feel like crap)
Comment: anything else: Thank you for working on this and listening to the community. It’s must be extremely hard, time consuming and mentally exhausting to work on a big project with so many opinions. As much as we complain, we really do appreciate it.

Comment: current building: This is related to some of the problems listed above, but I just want to frame it a different way. The main sanctuary used to be more equal in terms of space for women (the mechitza was closer to the Aron and the amud/shliach tzibur was therefore closer to the women's section). Understandably, as the men's section got more and more crowded, the mechitza was moved over. Both in terms of access to important spaces for anyone with disabilities, and in terms of ease of getting out of the building safely in event of an emergency. A new building would be an opportunity to address that properly.
I hope that the design of the new sanctuary space takes women's experience of shul seriously, which requires making sure to speak to the women who come to shul consistently.
